1. Core Clinical Tension: A newborn infant delivered precipitously to a Colombian mother who had experienced a transient febrile illness early in pregnancy, presenting with severe microcephaly, extensive craniofacial dysmorphism, intracranial calcifications, and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita. The severe congenital anomalies strongly mimic classic TORCH infections (such as CMV or toxoplasmosis) or primary monogenic microcephaly and syndromic brain malformation syndromes.
2. Admission Breakpoint: At neonatal birth triage and nursery admission following physical exam, neonatal growth measurements, and initial transfontanellar ultrasonography, immediately prior to send-out TORCH serologies, genetic karyotype/microarray, and maternal amniotic fluid RT-PCR.
3. Differential Distinctions: Cytomegalovirus and Toxoplasmosis typically produce periventricular or diffuse cerebral calcifications with chorioretinitis and systemic hepatosplenomegaly but lack severe craniofacial collapsing and arthrogryposis; monogenic primary microcephaly lacks placental and hepatic calcifications. Congenital Zika syndrome is confirmed by maternal-fetal RT-PCR and classic neuroimaging showing severe microcephaly, pachygyria, schizencephaly, and calcifications.
case_prompt:
A male infant was born precipitously in an ambulance at 38.6 weeks of gestation to a 28-year-old previously healthy Colombian woman traveling from a remote rural area. The mother had received late and irregular prenatal care. During her first trimester (at approximately 12 weeks of gestation), she experienced an acute illness lasting 2 to 7 days characterized by fever, myalgias, and vomiting. An antenatal ultrasound performed at 29.5 weeks of gestation had revealed multiple fetal anomalies including ventriculomegaly, suspected Arnold-Chiari malformation, hepatic calcifications, pyelocaliceal dilation, microcephaly, and apparent clubfoot.

At birth, the male newborn weighed 3,180 g (10th percentile), with a height of 48 cm (10th percentile) and a cephalic circumference of 31 cm (under the 2nd percentile). The mother reported that the newborn was irritable, with an abnormal pattern of crying and hyperexcitability. Physical examination showed distal tremors, hypertonia, trunk hyperextension, spasticity, increased deep tendon reflexes, persistent primitive responses, clenched fists, strabismus, and nystagmus. Craniofacial examination revealed microcephaly characterized by craniofacial disproportion, decreased vertical size of the skull, a sloping forehead, and pronounced supraorbital ridges, giving the appearance of oversized facial features and proptosis. Epicanthal folds, retrognathia, excess skin over the entire scalp and forehead, occipital and nuchal skin folds giving the appearance of a short neck, bilateral depressions of the forehead, and prominent overlapping metopic and sagittal sutures with supratemporal depressions were identified. Extremity examination revealed hand contractures, camptodactyly, feet contractures, prominent calcanei, multiple dimples, and arthrogryposis.

Transfontanelle ultrasonography demonstrated microcephaly, an increase of the width and number of the circumvolutions due to pachygyria, ventriculomegaly in the infratemporal and supratemporal fossae, closed-lip schizencephaly involving the left lateral ventricle, a cystic image in the posterior fossa communicating with the fourth ventricle, a thin corpus callosum, and pathological calcifications in the liver, brain (cortical and subcortical), and placenta.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Classical Congenital TORCH Infections (Cytomegalovirus, Toxoplasmosis, Rubella, Syphilis, HSV)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the leading cause of congenital microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and ventriculomegaly following maternal gestational fever; excluded by comprehensive serological testing.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: As part of the evaluation approach to a newborn with brain abnormalities, TORCH testing was performed to rule out the most frequent congenital infections (syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, cytomegalovirus, herpesvirus 1 and 2, and parvovirus B19) as causal etiology.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Primary Monogenic Microcephaly / Genetic Malformation Syndrome
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to severe craniofacial dysmorphism, overlapping sutures, arthrogryposis, and structural cortical malformations; prompted formal genetic evaluation, but the clinical spectrum was fully explained by vertical viral infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Because of the multiple abnormalities, a complete genetic assessment was performed on the newborn and his mother.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: First-trimester maternal febrile illness in an endemic region followed by detection of viral RNA by RT-PCR in amniotic fluid, together with pathognomonic neuroimaging findings of fetal disruption syndrome (severe microcephaly, pachygyria, schizencephaly, calcifications, and arthrogryposis), confirmed congenital Zika virus syndrome.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient had experienced an episode of illness for 2-7 days that was characterized by fever, myalgias, and vomiting. She went to the hospital, where ZIKV was presumed, and RT-PCR of the amniotic fluid was done, with a positive result at 12 weeks of gestation. The findings confirmed ZIKV vertical transmission and congenital infection.
